title: Trump Official Confronts Pakistani Event Manager Accused of Selling H-1B Visas
excerpt: The viral doorstep confrontation is part of a broader federal crackdown on H-1B visa fraud that has seen dozens of subpoenas and heightened scrutiny of the program.
body:
• A Trump administration official confronted Pakistani event manager Mohammad Abbas at his business, accusing him of selling H-1B visas through a shell event management company
  • The incident is part of a broader federal crackdown on H-1B visa fraud, with the Labor Department Inspector General confirming dozens of subpoenas have been served
  • The administration launched its first major H-1B fraud investigation targeting visa abuse, labour trafficking and displacement of American workers
  • Indian nationals hold 71% of all H-1B visas — making enforcement actions and program changes a direct concern for the diaspora

A Trump administration official showed up at the door of Mohammad Abbas, a Pakistani event manager in the United States, accusing him of running a fraudulent H-1B visa operation through his event management company. Video of the confrontation, in which the official declared "This right here is everything that's wrong with H-1Bs," went viral on social media and reignited debate over visa fraud and the integrity of America's skilled-worker immigration system.

Abbas is accused of sponsoring H-1B visa holders through his company without providing legitimate specialty-occupation work — effectively selling visa sponsorships to foreign nationals who paid for the chance to enter or remain in the United States on work permits.

How the Alleged Scheme Worked

H-1B visas require employers to demonstrate that they are hiring foreign workers for legitimate specialty occupations that require specialized knowledge. Fraudulent sponsors file petitions for positions that either don't exist or don't meet the program's requirements, charging workers fees in exchange for the paperwork needed to obtain or maintain visa status.

The Trump administration says these operations displace American workers, undercut wages and undermine the integrity of a program originally designed to bring in highly skilled talent for roles that U.S. employers genuinely cannot fill domestically.

Part of a Broader Federal Crackdown

The Abbas confrontation comes amid the administration's most aggressive enforcement push against H-1B fraud to date. Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito confirmed in a Fox Business interview that investigators have already served dozens of subpoenas as part of the first major federal H-1B fraud investigation.

"This is another example where fraud is fueling violent crime. Much of the visa and the human trafficking that we see when it comes to this foreign labor is tied to cartels, is tied to transnational gangs."

— Anthony D'Esposito, Labor Department Inspector General

The probe targets H-1B and PERM visa fraud, labour trafficking and the systematic displacement of qualified American workers. D'Esposito said the investigation extends beyond traditional workplace violations, with some alleged abuses occurring in medical facilities where unqualified workers could endanger patients.

Vice President JD Vance has also outlined the administration's wider anti-fraud initiative, framing it as central to the "America First" employment agenda.

H-1B Program Under Legal and Political Pressure

The enforcement action comes after a federal judge struck down the administration's $100,000 H-1B visa fee in June, ruling it amounted to an unauthorized tax. A First Circuit appeals court subsequently refused to stay that ruling, meaning the fee remains blocked while litigation continues.

Despite the legal setback on fees, the administration has tightened oversight through other channels. The State Department now requires consular officers to review LinkedIn profiles and resumes of H-1B applicants for involvement in content moderation or "censorship." Enhanced vetting has stranded some Indian visa holders abroad as appointment schedules were disrupted.

What It Means for Indian H-1B Holders

Indian nationals account for approximately 71% of all H-1B visa recipients, making them the single largest group affected by any changes to the program. While the fraud enforcement targets specific bad actors — not legitimate visa holders — immigration attorneys say the broader crackdown has created a chilling effect.

Anti-Indian hostility has surged alongside the policy changes. Threats of violence against South Asian communities rose 12% in November 2025, while online slurs targeting South Asians jumped 69% over the same period, according to an analysis by advocacy group Stop AAPI Hate and counterterrorism firm Moonshot.

For the millions of Indian professionals who hold or aspire to H-1B status, the Abbas case illustrates both the genuine fraud problems that exist within the system and the political environment in which all H-1B holders are increasingly scrutinized — regardless of whether they entered through legitimate channels.
